title: Agent2Agent Protocol and the Future of Agentic Workloads
objective: Frame the before/after story for A2A.
learnerQuestion: What problem does A2A solve for agentic workloads?
coreClaim: A2A standardizes the boundary where one agent delegates work to another and tracks task-native progress and outputs.
mechanism: Agent Card discovery plus message, task, status, and artifact operations.
example: Customer operations coordinator delegating to specialist agents.
counterpoint: A2A standardizes the boundary; it does not make weak agent design reliable.
practicalTakeaway: Think of A2A as an agent service boundary, not an internal prompt pattern.

title: What You Should Be Able To Reason About
learnerQuestion: What should I know before adopting A2A?
coreClaim: Adoption requires understanding task semantics, discovery, streaming/push, artifacts, framework adapters, security, and governance.
mechanism: A2A concepts become implementation responsibilities in clients, servers, registries, and observability.
example: Map a support handoff into Agent Card, task id, context id, events, and artifact validation.
counterpoint: Framework support does not remove architecture work.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate A2A with a production integration checklist.

title: Use A Customer Operations Workflow As The Thread
learnerQuestion: What concrete workflow will make A2A useful?
coreClaim: Customer operations exposes the need for specialist delegation, long-running work, artifacts, and human review.
mechanism: Coordinator delegates tasks to billing, support, data, and compliance agents.
example: Investigate a customer escalation and return a cited remediation artifact.
counterpoint: A simpler single-agent loop may not need A2A.
practicalTakeaway: Anchor protocol adoption in a real cross-agent workflow.

title: Agent Integration Usually Starts As Custom Glue
learnerQuestion: What does A2A replace?
coreClaim: Before A2A, teams usually invent custom agent APIs, tool wrappers, and state handoff conventions.
mechanism: Each integration defines its own discovery, task ids, progress, callbacks, and result shapes.
example: Coordinator hardcodes an HTTP endpoint for a billing agent.
counterpoint: Custom APIs can still be sufficient for narrow internal boundaries.
practicalTakeaway: Use A2A when bespoke glue is becoming repeated infrastructure.

title: The Hard Part Is Not HTTP; It Is Agent Semantics
learnerQuestion: Why is a normal REST endpoint not enough?
coreClaim: The hard part is representing agent capabilities, conversational messages, long-running tasks, intermediate state, and artifacts.
mechanism: A2A defines protocol objects for Agent Cards, Messages, Parts, Tasks, and Artifacts.
example: A compliance agent returns an input-required state before producing an artifact.
counterpoint: HTTP remains the binding, but semantics are the useful standard.
practicalTakeaway: Standardize agent semantics, not just endpoints.

title: Tool Wrappers Flatten Agent Behavior Into One Call
objective: Explain why tool-shaped wrapping is insufficient.
learnerQuestion: Why not expose every remote agent as a tool?
coreClaim: Tool wrappers hide an agent's ability to manage tasks, ask for input, stream progress, and return artifacts.
mechanism: A tool call typically has one request and one response, while A2A has task lifecycle state.
example: Support agent needs to ask a clarifying question before completing a diagnosis.
counterpoint: MCP tools remain appropriate for deterministic tool/context access.
practicalTakeaway: Use agent boundaries for autonomous delegated work.

title: A2A Standardizes How Agents Expose And Consume Delegated Work
learnerQuestion: What does A2A add to agent collaboration?
coreClaim: A2A gives agents a portable way to publish capabilities, accept messages, manage tasks, and return artifacts.
mechanism: Agent Card discovery plus message/send, task status, streaming, and artifact outputs.
example: A coordinator selects a remote data-analysis agent from its Agent Card.
counterpoint: The consuming app still owns trust, routing, and policy.
practicalTakeaway: Design A2A as a service contract.

title: The Layers Separate Data Model, Operations, And Binding
learnerQuestion: What parts of the protocol should I separate?
coreClaim: A2A separates objects, operations, and transport/framework bindings.
mechanism: Data model objects are mapped to HTTP/JSON-RPC operations and then adapted into framework runtimes.
example: A LangGraph thread can map to A2A context/task concepts through an adapter.
counterpoint: Framework mapping is not standardized uniformly across ecosystems.
practicalTakeaway: Keep protocol concepts separate from framework internals.

title: Learn These Nouns First
learnerQuestion: Which A2A terms matter most?
coreClaim: Agent Card, Message, Part, Task, Artifact, and capability declarations are the core vocabulary.
mechanism: Messages carry interaction payloads; tasks track delegated work; artifacts represent deliverables.
example: A task can produce a report artifact after several status events.
counterpoint: Domain-specific schema still sits above these protocol objects.
practicalTakeaway: Use protocol nouns precisely in design discussions.

title: The Card Is The Integration Handshake
learnerQuestion: How does a client know what a remote agent can do?
coreClaim: Agent Cards publish metadata, capabilities, skills, endpoints, and optional features for a remote agent.
mechanism: Clients fetch or receive an Agent Card and use it to decide whether and how to delegate work.
example: Agent Card declares streaming support and supported input/output modes.
counterpoint: Agent Cards need lifecycle and trust management; stale cards are a production risk.
practicalTakeaway: Treat Agent Cards like API product metadata.

title: Discovery Strategy Is An Architecture Decision
learnerQuestion: How should clients find agents?
coreClaim: Discovery can use known endpoints, registries, service catalogs, or domain-specific routing, each with trust and lifecycle tradeoffs.
mechanism: Discovery produces candidate Agent Cards that the client evaluates.
example: Internal registry for customer operations specialists.
counterpoint: The protocol does not mandate one universal registry.
practicalTakeaway: Design discovery alongside auth and governance.

title: A Request Becomes A Task, Then Events And Artifacts
learnerQuestion: What happens after a client delegates work?
coreClaim: Delegation becomes a task lifecycle with messages, state changes, streaming events, and artifacts.
mechanism: Send message -> create/update task -> emit status/artifact events -> complete or wait for input.
example: Billing agent streams investigation progress before returning an adjustment recommendation.
counterpoint: Clients must persist task correlation to survive disconnects.
practicalTakeaway: Model remote work as durable tasks.

title: A Minimal Portable Call Is Just Protocol-Shaped HTTP
learnerQuestion: Can I use A2A without a framework?
coreClaim: A2A can be called through standard protocol-shaped HTTP/JSON payloads.
mechanism: Client sends a message operation and parses task/message/artifact response structures.
example: Raw HTTP client invokes a remote agent endpoint.
counterpoint: Production clients still need auth, retries, streaming, and task persistence.
practicalTakeaway: Start small, but plan production client responsibilities.

title: Workloads Need To Handle Interrupted States, Not Only Success/Failure
learnerQuestion: Why is task state more complex than done/failed?
coreClaim: A2A tasks can represent working, input-required, canceled, rejected, failed, and completed states.
mechanism: Task state is reported through status and event updates.
example: Compliance agent enters input-required for human approval.
counterpoint: State names alone do not define your business workflow.
practicalTakeaway: Build UI and persistence for interrupted task states.

title: Choose Polling, Streaming, Or Push By Workload Shape
learnerQuestion: How should clients receive task progress?
coreClaim: Polling, streaming, and push notifications fit different connection and latency requirements.
mechanism: Polling checks task state; streaming holds a connected event stream; push notifies a webhook-like receiver.
example: Long compliance review uses push, while interactive chat uses streaming.
counterpoint: Push introduces webhook security and delivery reliability concerns.
practicalTakeaway: Choose delivery mode from user experience and reliability needs.

title: Messages Are Conversation; Artifacts Are Deliverables
learnerQuestion: What should go in a message versus an artifact?
coreClaim: Messages carry conversational interaction while artifacts represent task outputs that can be reviewed, stored, and validated.
mechanism: Task events can include message updates and artifact outputs.
example: Agent asks a clarifying question as a message and returns a remediation plan as an artifact.
counterpoint: Your domain schema controls artifact validation.
practicalTakeaway: Do not bury deliverables in chat text.

title: A2A Delegates Auth To Standard Web Security, But Composition Raises The Bar
learnerQuestion: What security work remains?
coreClaim: A2A relies on standard web security patterns, while multi-agent composition adds authorization, delegation, and artifact trust concerns.
mechanism: Agent endpoints need authn/authz, policy checks, scoped credentials, and audit trails.
example: Coordinator can call billing agent only for accounts the user may access.
counterpoint: Protocol support does not automatically prove identity or authority across organizations.
practicalTakeaway: Design delegated authorization explicitly.

title: Use MCP For Tools; Use A2A For Peer Agents
learnerQuestion: When should I use MCP versus A2A?
coreClaim: MCP is for tools/resources/context; A2A is for peer agents that own delegated work.
mechanism: An A2A agent can internally call MCP tools while exposing task-native collaboration externally.
example: Support agent uses MCP to query logs, then exposes A2A to the coordinator.
counterpoint: Some simple remote capabilities are better tools than agents.
practicalTakeaway: Choose boundary by autonomy and task lifecycle.

title: The System Becomes A Network Of Capability-Owning Agents
learnerQuestion: What does an A2A architecture look like?
coreClaim: A2A enables a coordinator to delegate to remote specialist agents that own capabilities and task state.
mechanism: Coordinator discovers Agent Cards, delegates tasks, receives events/artifacts, and composes outputs.
example: Customer operations routes billing, compliance, and support tasks to different agents.
counterpoint: The coordinator still owns policy, UX, and final response assembly.
practicalTakeaway: Use A2A for capability ownership across boundaries.

title: The After Is Not Magic; It Moves Responsibilities
learnerQuestion: What new work does A2A create?
coreClaim: A2A shifts integration work into registry, auth, task persistence, tracing, artifact validation, and lifecycle governance.
mechanism: Protocol objects need production storage, policy, and observability around them.
example: Persist task ids and artifacts for audit and retry.
counterpoint: The standard reduces bespoke shape, not operational responsibility.
practicalTakeaway: Budget for the platform layer around A2A.

title: A2A Fits Best At Service Boundaries, Not Inside Every Loop
learnerQuestion: Where should I not use A2A?
coreClaim: A2A is strongest when agents cross ownership or service boundaries, not for every internal reasoning step.
mechanism: Protocol overhead pays off when discovery, delegation, task state, and artifacts matter.
example: Use direct graph nodes inside one LangGraph workflow; use A2A for a remote specialist service.
counterpoint: Internal use can still help if teams need strict agent product boundaries.
practicalTakeaway: Use A2A at meaningful ownership boundaries.

title: Practical Adoption Is A Wrapping And Governance Exercise
learnerQuestion: How do I retrofit an existing agent?
coreClaim: Adoption usually wraps existing runtime state and tools into A2A messages, tasks, streaming, artifacts, and auth.
mechanism: Adapter maps framework input/output, state, cancellation, and tracing to protocol objects.
example: Expose a graph-based support agent as an A2A server.
counterpoint: Poorly designed adapters leak framework assumptions into the protocol boundary.
practicalTakeaway: Design adapters around protocol semantics, not just transport.

title: Support Exists, But It Is Not Uniform
learnerQuestion: Can I plug A2A into existing frameworks?
coreClaim: Framework support exists across several ecosystems, but feature depth and mapping differ.
mechanism: Some expose A2A endpoints; others provide remote-agent wrappers or examples.
example: LangChain Agent Server, Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, and Mastra support A2A in different ways.
counterpoint: Version drift is high; verify current docs before implementation.
practicalTakeaway: Treat framework support as a starting point, not a complete architecture.

title: Expose Message-Based Graph State As An A2A-Compatible Agent
learnerQuestion: How does graph state map to A2A?
coreClaim: Message-based graph state can be exposed through an A2A endpoint by mapping context, thread, messages, and streaming events.
mechanism: LangChain Agent Server maps A2A contextId to thread_id for tracing/runtime continuity.
example: Remote graph agent streams progress to an A2A client.
counterpoint: Graph-specific state should not leak into portable artifacts unnecessarily.
practicalTakeaway: Make the protocol boundary message/task-native.

title: ADK Shows The Value Of Local Plus Remote Agents
learnerQuestion: What does A2A look like in Google ADK?
coreClaim: ADK documents local and remote agent patterns that let one agent interact with another through A2A.
mechanism: A local agent can expose or consume A2A-compatible remote agents.
example: Coordinator delegates to a remote ADK agent.
counterpoint: ADK's integration pattern is not identical to every framework.
practicalTakeaway: Use framework-native helpers where they preserve protocol semantics.

title: Newer Framework Support Turns A2A Into A Delegation Option
learnerQuestion: Is A2A becoming a common framework boundary?
coreClaim: A2A support in frameworks turns remote agents into delegation targets, but support remains uneven.
mechanism: Frameworks provide endpoint serving, remote agent clients, continuation tokens, or delegation adapters.
example: Microsoft Agent Framework exposes A2A provider patterns.
counterpoint: Check current framework docs before relying on a feature.
practicalTakeaway: Track framework support as part of architecture selection.

title: Every Framework Still Has To Bridge The Same Concepts
learnerQuestion: What must every adapter map?
coreClaim: Adapters must bridge messages, task ids, context ids, state, streaming, artifacts, cancellation, auth, and tracing.
mechanism: Runtime-specific state is translated into A2A protocol objects and operations.
example: A CrewAI or Mastra agent needs task and artifact mapping just like a LangGraph agent.
counterpoint: Some frameworks may not expose every needed lifecycle hook cleanly.
practicalTakeaway: Design adapters with a concept mapping table.

title: A Portable Client Has Five Responsibilities
learnerQuestion: What does an A2A client need to do?
coreClaim: A portable client discovers cards, sends messages, tracks tasks, consumes events, validates artifacts, and handles auth/errors.
mechanism: Client state stores context/task ids and delivery mode state.
example: Coordinator reconnects to a task stream after network interruption.
counterpoint: SDKs help but do not design application state.
practicalTakeaway: Implement durable client correlation early.

title: The Coordinator Becomes A Runtime Router, Not A Giant Prompt
learnerQuestion: How does A2A change coordinator design?
coreClaim: A coordinator selects capability-owning agents and manages delegation lifecycle rather than embedding every specialist behavior in one prompt.
mechanism: Agent Card selection plus task creation, event handling, and artifact composition.
example: Coordinator routes billing questions to billing agent and policy questions to compliance agent.
counterpoint: Routing policy can become complex and must be observable.
practicalTakeaway: Make routing decisions explicit and traceable.

title: Long-Running Delegation Needs Durable Correlation
learnerQuestion: Why persist task and context ids?
coreClaim: Long-running tasks require durable correlation across reconnects, polling, push callbacks, retries, and audit.
mechanism: Store task id, context id, remote agent id, user scope, state, and artifact references.
example: A compliance review completes after the user closes the browser.
counterpoint: In-memory task state is fragile for production.
practicalTakeaway: A2A workloads need a task store.

title: A2A Transports Structured Data, But It Does Not Design Your Domain Schema
learnerQuestion: Does A2A define my business payloads?
coreClaim: A2A provides protocol structure; domain schemas, artifact contracts, and validation remain application responsibilities.
mechanism: Parts and artifacts carry data, but the domain decides shape, constraints, and meaning.
example: RemediationPlan artifact schema with severity, steps, owners, and citations.
counterpoint: Without domain schema, artifacts become unreviewable blobs.
practicalTakeaway: Define artifact schemas alongside the protocol boundary.

title: A2A Makes Human-In-The-Loop And Slow Operations First-Class
learnerQuestion: How does A2A help with human approval and slow work?
coreClaim: Task states and async delivery make input-required and slow operations explicit.
mechanism: Task status can reflect waiting for input while clients poll, stream, or receive push notification.
example: Agent waits for a manager approval before completing refund recommendation.
counterpoint: The protocol does not design approval policy or UI.
practicalTakeaway: Represent waiting as state, not as hidden blocking.

title: Agent Networks Fail Differently Than Single-Agent Apps
learnerQuestion: What new failures does A2A introduce?
coreClaim: Agent networks add failures around discovery, remote availability, partial artifacts, duplicate tasks, stale cards, and policy conflicts.
mechanism: Each remote task boundary creates network, trust, state, and lifecycle failure points.
example: Billing agent accepts task but never returns final artifact.
counterpoint: A2A makes many failures observable if task state is tracked well.
practicalTakeaway: Design retries, cancellation, and fallback per delegated task.

title: Trace The Protocol Boundary, Not Only The Model Call
learnerQuestion: What should I trace in A2A systems?
coreClaim: Observability must track discovery, message send, task id, status events, artifacts, errors, auth, and remote latency.
mechanism: Trace spans should cross the A2A boundary and correlate local workflow state with remote task state.
example: Link coordinator trace to LangSmith thread or remote task id.
counterpoint: Model-call traces alone miss remote task lifecycle failures.
practicalTakeaway: Trace tasks and artifacts, not just prompts.

title: A2A Makes Agent Publishing Look More Like API Product Management
learnerQuestion: What does it mean to publish an A2A agent?
coreClaim: Published agents need versioned cards, documented skills, auth policy, supported modes, limits, and change management.
mechanism: Agent Card metadata becomes the product contract consumers rely on.
example: Deprecate an old billing skill with a card version update.
counterpoint: Internal-only agents still need lifecycle rules if multiple teams consume them.
practicalTakeaway: Manage Agent Cards like APIs.

title: To Benefit From A2A, Workloads Need To Become Task-Native
learnerQuestion: How must workloads evolve to use A2A well?
coreClaim: Workloads need explicit task ids, state transitions, artifact contracts, cancellation, durable correlation, and async UX.
mechanism: Business workflow maps onto A2A task lifecycle rather than one blocking function call.
example: Customer escalation moves from submitted to working to input-required to completed with artifacts.
counterpoint: If work is immediate and deterministic, a tool call may be simpler.
practicalTakeaway: Adopt A2A when you can model work as tasks.

title: A2A Does Not Fix Weak Agent Design
learnerQuestion: What problems will A2A not solve?
coreClaim: A2A does not fix poor prompts, missing tools, bad retrieval, weak evals, unsafe policies, or unreliable domain logic.
mechanism: The protocol transports requests and outputs; quality depends on the underlying agent system.
example: A low-quality compliance agent can return a bad artifact through a valid A2A task.
counterpoint: Protocol structure can make failures more visible and testable.
practicalTakeaway: Validate agent quality independently of protocol compatibility.

title: Expect A Mixed World For A While
learnerQuestion: Will every framework support A2A equally?
coreClaim: A2A adoption will coexist with custom APIs, MCP tools, framework-native runtimes, and partial adapters.
mechanism: Different frameworks expose A2A at different depths and maturity levels.
example: LangChain, ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, and Mastra have different integration patterns.
counterpoint: Mixed integration does not eliminate A2A value at selected boundaries.
practicalTakeaway: Plan adapters and fallback paths.

title: Should This Boundary Use A2A?
learnerQuestion: When should I choose A2A?
coreClaim: Use A2A when the remote capability is agentic, taskful, independently owned, long-running, or artifact-producing.
mechanism: Decision criteria include ownership boundary, autonomy, task lifecycle, streaming/push need, artifact output, and governance.
example: Remote compliance review agent qualifies; a deterministic calculator likely does not.
counterpoint: Protocol overhead may be unnecessary inside a tight local workflow.
practicalTakeaway: Choose A2A deliberately, not by default.

title: What To Implement For A Production A2A Agent
learnerQuestion: What does a production A2A server need?
coreClaim: Production agents need Agent Card lifecycle, auth, task store, streaming/push handling, artifact schemas, observability, cancellation, and policy.
mechanism: Protocol operations are backed by durable state, adapters, guards, and monitoring.
example: Persist task status and artifact URLs for customer escalation workflow.
counterpoint: SDK scaffolds do not replace production platform work.
practicalTakeaway: Build the platform around the protocol.

title: Before And After For Customer Operations
objective: Apply the model to anchor workflow.
learnerQuestion: How does the anchor workflow change with A2A?
coreClaim: Customer operations moves from hardcoded specialist calls to discoverable, task-tracked remote agents with artifacts.
mechanism: Coordinator selects specialists by Agent Card, creates tasks, streams progress, receives artifacts, and composes final response.
example: Billing, data, and compliance agents each return scoped artifacts.
counterpoint: The coordinator still owns UX, escalation policy, and final accountability.
practicalTakeaway: A2A changes integration architecture, not business responsibility.

title: The Mental Model
learnerQuestion: What is the one model to keep?
coreClaim: Before A2A, agents are isolated apps or tool wrappers; A2A gives a standard delegation contract; after A2A, workloads become distributed task systems.
mechanism: Discovery, task lifecycle, streaming/push, artifacts, auth, and observability form the boundary.
example: Coordinator delegates and tracks a support investigation as a task with artifacts.
counterpoint: Distributed task systems need governance and failure handling.
practicalTakeaway: Think task-native, not call-native.

title: Follow-up Reading
learnerQuestion: Where should I verify current A2A details?
coreClaim: The A2A protocol docs are the source of truth; framework docs show current adapter support.
mechanism: References are grouped by protocol concepts, framework support, and SDKs.
example: Use the A2A spec for task states and LangChain/ADK/Microsoft docs for framework-specific integration.
counterpoint: A2A and framework support are version-sensitive.
practicalTakeaway: Re-check sources before implementation.
